When Is Thinking Enough? Early Exit via Sufficiency Assessment for
Efficient Reasoning
Yang Xiang1, Yixin Ji1, Ruotao Xu1, Dan Qiao2, Zheming Yang2, Juntao Li1*, Min Zhang1,3
1Soochow University 2ByteDance
3Key Laboratory of General Artificial Intelligence and Large Models, Soochow University

Abstract
Large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved
remarkable performance in complex reasoning
tasks, driven by their powerful inference-time
scaling capability. However, LRMs often suffer
from overthinking, which results in substantial
computational redundancy and significantly re-
duces efficiency. Early-exit methods aim to mit-
igate this issue by terminating reasoning once
sufficient evidence has been generated, yet ex-
isting approaches mostly rely on handcrafted or
empirical indicators that are unreliable and im-
practical. In this work, we introduceDynamic
Thought Sufficiency in Reasoning (DTSR),
a novel framework for efficient reasoning that
enables the model to dynamically assess the
sufficiency of its chain-of-thought (CoT) and
determine the optimal point for early exit. In-
spired by human metacognition, DTSR oper-
ates in two stages: (1)Reflection Signal Mon-
itoring, which identifies reflection signals as
potential cues for early exit, and (2)Thought
Sufficiency Check, which evaluates whether the
current CoT is sufficient to derive the final an-
swer. Experimental results on the Qwen3 mod-
els show that DTSR reduces reasoning length
by 28.9%–34.9% with minimal performance
loss, effectively mitigating overthinking. We
further discuss overconfidence in LRMs and
self-evaluation paradigms, providing valuable
insights for early-exit reasoning.
1 Introduction
The success of large reasoning models (LRMs),
such as OpenAI’s o1/o4 (OpenAI, 2024, 2025),
Gemini 2.5 Pro (Comanici et al., 2025), DeepSeek-
R1 (Guo et al., 2025), and Qwen3 (Yang et al.,
2025a), represents a significant breakthrough in the
evolution of LLMs. LRMs engage in long chain-of-
thought (CoT) reasoning before producing answers.
The inference-time scaling capability (Chen et al.,
2025a; Ji et al., 2025) allows them to achieve re-
markable performance in challenging reasoning

tasks (e.g. mathematics, programming, and sci-
entific question answering), and show human-like
reasoning patterns, such as problem decomposition,
verification and backtracking.
Nevertheless, recent studies (Chen et al., 2025b;
Cuadron et al., 2025) have shown that LRMs often
suffer from overthinking: even on simple prob-
lems, they tend to consume excessive tokens by re-
peatedly verifying answers or exploring alternative
strategies after reaching the correct solution. Such
redundant reasoning is unnecessary and leads to in-
efficiency. To address this, several prior works have
proposed early-exit strategies that stop the reason-
ing process once the LRM has generated sufficient
evidence to solve the problem. The main challenge
of early-exit strategies is to determine the optimal
exit point, where LRMs achieve near-lossless per-
formance with minimal reasoning cost. Dynasor-
CoT (Fu et al., 2025) first employs the consistency
of intermediate answers to determine when to exit
reasoning; however, it still generates additional to-
ken intervals after producing the correct answer
to verify its correctness, thereby missing the op-
timal exit point. DEER (Yang et al., 2025b) and
CGRS (Huang et al., 2025) employ the entropy of
the intermediate result as a confidence measure to
determine whether LRMs reach the optimal exit
point. Nevertheless, using answer confidence as a
criterion for reasoning exit is not always reliable,
as reasoning models can exhibit overconfidence
even when their answers are incorrect (Mei et al.,
2025). Moreover, such methods that rely on prob-
ing intermediate answers are limited to tasks with
short, fixed-format answers. For tasks involving
long answers or open-ended generation without a
definitive answer, intermediate answers are difficult
to extract, rendering these methods impractical.
To overcome these limitations, this work aims to
establish a reliable and generalizable criterion for
early-exit. Unlike LLM reasoning, human cogni-
tion involves metacognitive (Flavell, 1979; Fleur
23541

et al., 2021) abilities, which allow people to mon-
itor, evaluate, and regulate their thoughts, and to
stop thinking once the process is deemed sufficient.
Inspired by this, we wonder whether LRMs can
similarly determine the optimal point to exit rea-
soning by continuously assessing the sufficiency
of their current thoughts? To answer this, we pro-
pose Dynamic Thought Sufficiency in Reasoning
(DTSR), a novel framework that enables models
to dynamically evaluate whether their current CoT
is sufficient to solve the problem. DTSR consists
of two stages: 1) Reflection Signal Monitoring:
LRMs often exhibit reflective behaviors after pro-
ducing an answer, typically triggered by specific
reflection signals. We identify these signals as po-
tential exit points for reasoning. 2) Thought Suffi-
ciency Check: once a reflection signal is detected,
the model evaluates the sufficiency of its current
reasoning. If the sufficiency score is high, reason-
ing stops and the solution is output; otherwise, the
model continues along the reasoning path until the
next reflection signal occurs.
To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed
method, we conducted extensive experiments
across multiple LRMs. The results show that DTSR
significantly outperforms baseline approaches,
achieving a favorable balance between accuracy
and efficiency. This also demonstrates that rea-
soning models can reliably assess the sufficiency
of their thought, providing valuable insights and
guidance for advancing efficient reasoning.
Overall, our contributions are as follows:
• We propose a novel framework for efficient rea-
soning that enables the model to dynamically
assess the sufficiency of its CoT and determine
the optimal point for early exit.
• Extensive experiments conducted on Qwen3 se-
ries models of various sizes demonstrate that
DTSR consistently outperforms baseline meth-
ods, achieving a 28.9%–34.9% reduction in gen-
eration length with almost no loss in performance,
thereby significantly mitigating overthinking.
• Further discussion of overconfidence in LRMs
and the self-evaluation paradigm offers a fresh
perspective and valuable insights for guiding
early-exit reasoning.
2 Methodology
2.1 Preliminaries
Generation Patterns of Reasoning ModelsThe
responses of LRMs are typically structured in two
stages: a reasoning phase, in which the model en-
gages in slow, human-like thinking, encapsulated
within the <think> and </think> delimiters, fol-
lowed by a solution phase that summarizes the
reasoning and produces the final answer. During
the thinking process, the model exhibits complex
reasoning behaviors, such as problem decomposi-
tion, strategy exploration, output verification, and
self-correction (Gandhi et al., 2025; Bogdan et al.,
2025). To trigger these reflective behaviors, LRMs
often generate tokens like “Wait”, “Alternatively”,
or “Let me check” as cues. However, once the
correct answer has been reached, further verifica-
tion becomes redundant, leading to unnecessary
reasoning cost (Chen et al., 2025b).
Early Exit in ReasoningEarly exit is a promis-
ing strategy for mitigating redundant reasoning.
Muennighoff et al. (2025) first introduces a simple
budget forcing method: when generation reaches
the maximum token budget, the model is forced to
append the end-of-thinking token and “Final An-
swer:” to terminate reasoning and output its current
answer. Dynasor-CoT (Fu et al., 2025) probes in-
termediate answers via designed prompts at fixed
intervals and terminates reasoning once consecu-
tive answers are consistent. It partially mitigates
overthinking but still generates extra token inter-
vals to verify correctness after the correct answer
is produced, failing to achieve optimal exit point.
In contrast, DEER (Yang et al., 2025b) outputs in-
termediate answers at reasoning transition points
(e.g., “Wait”) and uses entropy to estimate their con-
fidence, terminating the reasoning process when
achieving high confidence.
However, previous methods mainly rely on hand-
crafted or statistical criteria, which are unreliable
for determining whether the current reasoning pro-
cess is sufficient to yield the correct answer. Mei
et al. (2025) find that even state-of-the-art reason-
ing models are overconfident, particularly for incor-
rect answers, and this overconfidence grows with
the longer reasoning process. Consequently, a sub-
stantial gap exists between token probabilities and
the actual correctness of answers. From a cognitive
perspective, humans rarely produce explicit inter-
mediate answers to decide when to stop thinking.
Instead, through metacognitive processes (Fleur
et al., 2021), they internally assess whether their
thoughts are sufficient to reach a final answer. In-
spired by this, enabling reasoning models to self-
assess the sufficiency of their thought to determine

2.2 Our Proposal: Dynamic Thought
Sufficiency in Reasoning
As shown in Figure 1, we present DTSR, a method
that enables the model to dynamically evaluate the
sufficiency of its reasoning process. Our method
consists of two stages: reflection signal monitoring
and thought sufficiency check.
Reflection Signal MonitoringOur objective is
to exit the reasoning process at the optimal point.
Since assessing thought sufficiency after every gen-
erated token is computationally impractical, we
instead seek to identify potential exit signals that
indicate when verification should be triggered. To
this end, we conduct an empirical analysis of rea-
soning trajectories generated by Qwen3-32B. For
each trajectory, we identify its optimal early-exit
point, defined as the earliest position in the reason-
ing process at which the model is already capable
of producing a correct answer (Figure 7). We find
that these optimal exit points are often followed
by explicit self-reflection or answer-verification be-
haviors, manifested through cues such as “Wait”,
“Alternatively”, and phrases beginning with “But”
(e.g., “But wait”, “But let me check”). Based on
these observations, we construct a reflection signal
set, the complete list of which is shown in Table 4.
Thought Sufficiency CheckThe LRM continues
reasoning until a reflection signal is encountered.
Upon detecting such a signal, the model performs
a thought sufficiency check on the reasoning trace
generated so far to determine whether it can ter-
minate further thinking and produce a final solu-
tion. Specifically, at each checkpoint, the original
question together with the current chain-of-thought
(CoT) is fed into a dedicated thought sufficiency
check prompt template (shown in Figure 8). The
model is then prompted to generate a scalar score
indicating the sufficiency of the current reasoning.
A score exceeding the thresholdτindicates that the
model deems its reasoning sufficient; in this case,
we append a termination marker </think> to halt
further reasoning and allow the model to output the
final answer. Conversely, if the score falls below
the thresholdτ, the reasoning is considered insuffi-
cient, and the model resumes generation from the
last reflection signal, continuing the reasoning pro-
cess until the next checkpoint. This procedure is
repeated until the reasoning process is complete.
Unlike prior approaches that rely on handcrafted
heuristics or empirical external metrics, our method
determines the reasoning exit point through the
model’s internal self-evaluation. In this paradigm,
the model assesses the sufficiency of its previously
generated reasoning from a third-person perspec-
tive, treating the reasoning trace as an external ob-
ject rather than directly evaluating itself. Further
discussion of this can be found in Section 4.4.
Moreover, reflection signals frequently occur
in close succession, causing repeated sufficiency
checks to yield similar outcomes and resulting in
redundant computation. To mitigate this issue, we
enforce a minimum token intervalk between con-
secutive sufficiency checks. Concretely, a reflec-
tion signal triggers a thought sufficiency check only
if at leastk tokens have been generated since the
previous check; otherwise, the current signal is
skipped and the process continues (Algorithm 1).

3 Experiments
3.1 Experimental Setup
Benchmarks and MetricsTo comprehensively
evaluate the reasoning capabilities of LRMs, we se-
lect six widely used benchmarks: GSM8K (Cobbe
et al., 2021), MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021),
AMC 2023, OlympiadBench (He et al., 2024),
GPQA Diamond (Rein et al., 2024) and Live-
CodeBench (Jain et al., 2025). Our goal is to sig-
nificantly reduce the number of tokens generated
during the reasoning process while maintaining
high reasoning performance. To this end, we em-
ploy two primary metrics: Accuracy (Acc) and
Token Count (Tok). Acc measures the proportion
of correct final answers, calculated as the average
pass@1 score, whereas Tok represents the average
number of tokens generated per sample, serving as
an indicator of reasoning efficiency.
ModelsWe conduct extensive experiments on
the Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025a) series of models.
Our selection spans different model sizes (8B, 14B,
32B) of reasoning models to validate the generaliz-
ability of our method. Despite their strong reason-
ing ability, these models often exhibit overthinking
during the reasoning process.
BaselinesWe compare DTSR with the vanilla
LRM as well as existing state-of-the-art training-
free efficient reasoning methods, including No-
Thinking (Ma et al., 2025a), NOW AIT (Wang et al.,
2025), and DEER (Yang et al., 2025b). Vanilla
allows the model to generate answers directly with-
out any intervention. NoThinking prompts the
model to skip the reasoning stage and answer the
question directly. NOWAIT suppresses explicit
self-reflection by masking reflective tokens such
as “wait” and “hmm” during the reasoning process.
DEER makes early-exit decisions based on the con-
fidence scores of intermediate answers. In addition,
we compare DTSR with recent training-based meth-
ods (Arora and Zanette, 2025a; Dai et al., 2025).
Implementation DetailsAll experiments are
conducted using the vLLM framework to ensure
high throughput and memory-efficient inference.
For the decoding strategy, we set the temperature
to 0.6 and top-p to 0.95. The maximum genera-
tion length is set to 16k tokens, and each dataset
is generated three times, with the final results re-
ported as the average pass@1. In our method, the
thought sufficiency thresholdτis set to 100, and
the minimum token intervalkis set to 64.
3.2 Experimental Results
Overall PerformanceThe results in Table 1
show that DTSR consistently outperforms the base-
line methods across three model sizes and five
benchmark datasets. Compared with vanilla rea-
soning models, DTSR achieves almost the same
level of accuracy without any degradation, while re-
ducing sequence length by 28.9%–34.9%, leading
to more efficient inference. Notably, when applied
to Qwen3-14B, DTSR even improves performance
on challenging reasoning tasks such as GPQA and
OlympiadBench, underscoring its effectiveness.
Comparison with SOTAsWe compare DTSR
with several recent training-free efficient reasoning
methods. As shown in Table 1, DTSR effectively
shortens reasoning length without compromising
accuracy, whereas other baselines struggle to bal-
ance efficiency with performance. For instance, No-
Thinking enforces models to bypass the reasoning
process through prompting, which indeed shortens
sequences but deviates from the natural generation
paradigm and severely limits reasoning capability.
NoWAIT mitigates redundant output by masking
frequent reflective tokens, yet this restriction on the
model’s inherent self-reflection results in signifi-
cant performance degradation on complex reason-
ing tasks. DEER relies on the confidence scores
of intermediate answers, yet models often exhibit

Impact of token intervalk To begin with, vary-
ing the token interval k has almost no effect on
accuracy, since the criterion for assessing thought
sufficiency remains unchanged. Instead,k primar-

nearly constant. However, oncek>64 , the length
starts to increase ask grows. This occurs because
overly large token intervals may cause the model
to miss the optimal exit points for certain problems,
thereby delaying exit. Regarding latency, an over-
all U-shaped trend can be observed. When k≤64,
the reasoning latency increases due to the frequent
thought-sufficiency checks required at smaller in-
tervals. In contrast, when k >64 , although the
number of checks is reduced, the model tends to
generate longer reasoning traces after missing opti-
mal exit points, which in turn leads to increased la-
tency. Consequently,k= 64 represents a balanced
trade-off between generation length and latency,
making it a desirable choice in practice.

Impact of threshold τ Figure 5 presents the
performance of DTSR on the MATH-500 dataset
across different threshold values of τ. When the

which the model shows strong confidence in the
sufficiency of its reasoning process.
4.2 Analysis of Inference Latency
Table 2 reports the end-to-end inference latency of
DTSR on the MATH-500 and AMC datasets. The
results show that our method not only substantially
reduces the generation length, but also achieves a
significant reduction in inference latency, yielding
improvements of approximately 25%–40%. In con-
trast, although DEER reduces the final generation
length, it unexpectedly increases inference latency.
This performance gap can be attributed to two key
factors. First, we enable the continuous batching
strategy in vLLM, which allows different samples
to interleave between the generation and evaluation
phases. In contrast, DEER adopts a synchronous
scheme that requires all samples to complete gen-
eration before a collective evaluation, resulting in

Here, we discuss the issue of overconfidence in

after producing a trial answer. To further investi-
gate this issue, we derive two variants from DEER:
• DEER-1:The early-exit decision is based solely
on the confidence score of the trial answer.
• DEER-2:Whether the model generates
</think> after producing an intermediate an-
swer is used as the criterion for early exit.

solely on the confidence score of a trial answer is
insufficient for determining when to exit reason-

criterion of whether </think> is generated, attains

5 Related work
Recently, Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have
demonstrated remarkable performance on com-
plex reasoning tasks by generating long Chains
of Thought (CoT) for deep reasoning (Jaech et al.,
2024; Guo et al., 2025). However, recent stud-
ies (Chen et al., 2025b; Cuadron et al., 2025) have
revealed the issue of overthinking, where models
continue to reason even after obtaining the cor-
rect answer, leading to redundant computational
overhead. To address this, prior research has ex-
plored a variety of approaches to enable efficient
reasoning (Feng et al., 2025), which can be broadly
categorized into three directions: (Input) prompt-
guided methods, (Model) post-training methods,
and (Output) decoding-intervention methods.
Prompt-guided MethodsSuch methods lever-
age carefully designed prompts to guide the
model in performing efficient reasoning. Concise
CoT (Renze and Guven, 2024) simply adds the
instruction “Be concise” to the prompt, whereas
TALE (Han et al., 2025) first estimates an opti-
mal token budget and then incorporates it into
the prompt to encourage shorter reasoning chains.
Chain-of-Draft (Xu et al., 2025a) constrains the
model to preserve only the most essential reasoning
drafts at each step, thereby reducing token usage
in few-shot settings. Although easy to implement,
these approaches (Lee et al., 2025) are limited in
compressing long reasoning chains, and therefore
better suited for use alongside other methods.
Post-training MethodsThese methods typi-
cally employ supervised fine-tuning (SFT) using
variable-length CoT data (Yu et al., 2024; Liu et al.,
2024; Ma et al., 2025b), or leverage reinforcement
learning (RL) with length-based rewards (Team
et al., 2025; Arora and Zanette, 2025b; Yeo et al.,
2025; Yi et al., 2025). L1 (Aggarwal and Welleck,
2025) and Elastic Reasoning (Xu et al., 2025b)
incorporate length constraints into the reward func-
tion, training models to flexibly adjust the length
of reasoning chains under different token budgets.
Recently, numerous studies (Lou et al., 2025; Jiang
et al., 2025b; Fang et al., 2025) have focused on
training hybrid reasoning models that adaptively
choose between concise responses and long-chain
reasoning based on task complexity. While these
methods attempt to address the problem at the fun-
damental level, their high training costs restrict
most experiments to smaller models (e.g., 1.5B or
7B), limiting their applicability to larger models.
Decoding-intervention MethodsSuch methods
intervene during decoding to adjust generation,
guiding models to produce answers earlier (Qiao
et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025) or exit reason-
ing sooner (Liu and Wang, 2025; Jiang et al.,
2025a; Zhang et al., 2025). NoW AIT (Wang et al.,
2025) attempts to suppress explicit self-reflection
by blocking tokens like Wait and Hmm during rea-
soning. However, the model can readily bypass this
restriction by generating other tokens. Dynasor-
CoT (Fu et al., 2025) probes the model’s inter-
mediate answers at fixed token intervals and stops
thinking if three consecutive answers are consistent,
whereas DEER (Yang et al., 2025b) tracks interme-
diate answers at reasoning transition points and de-
termines whether to terminate reasoning based on
their confidence scores. However, both approaches
rely on probing intermediate answers to determine
stopping points, which works well only for prob-
lems with definite answers, but is less effective for
long-form or open-ended outputs. In contrast, our
approach effectively overcomes this limitation.
6 Conclusion
In this work, we alleviate the inefficiency of LRMs
by introducing Dynamic Thought Sufficiency in
Reasoning (DTSR), a novel framework that en-
ables models to dynamically determine when their
CoT is sufficient to yield a reliable answer. By in-
tegrating reflection signal monitoring with thought
sufficiency checks, DTSR provides a principled
mechanism for mitigating overthinking while main-
taining strong reasoning performance. Experiments
on Qwen3 models demonstrate that DTSR achieves
substantial reductions in reasoning length with
only minimal performance degradation, highlight-
ing its effectiveness in improving efficiency. We
further discuss overconfidence in LRMs and the
self-evaluation paradigm, shedding light on how
models effectively assess the sufficiency of their
CoT. This exploration offers a fresh perspective and
valuable insights for guiding early-exit reasoning.

While DTSR demonstrates promising results in
improving reasoning efficiency, we identify some
possible limitations as follows.

• This work focuses exclusively on textual reason-

have not yet extended our method to multimodal
reasoning or agent scenarios, which we leave for
